1.topic: Measurement, the scientific method and the structure of the atom
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. measure mass, length, time, temperature and volume with the right instrument and SI unit;
2. state the number of significant figures in a reading and tell precision from accuracy;
3. outline the steps of the scientific method;
4. give a short account of the atomic models of Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr;
5. work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from the symbol of an atom.

## Materials

A top-loading balance, a metre rule, a stopwatch, a thermometer, a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder and a burette, a chart of the atomic models, a chart of the first twenty elements.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask three students to read the same volume of water in the measuring cylinder and write their readings on the board. Ask: why are the readings not all the same, and which one is right?

## Development

1. Show each instrument and the quantity and SI unit it measures. Demonstrate reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
2. Explain significant figures with burette readings (24.50 cm³ has four). Use target diagrams to separate precision (readings close together) from accuracy (readings close to the true value).
3. Write the scientific method as a flow: observation, hypothesis, experiment, law, theory.
4. Use the chart to take the class through Dalton's solid atom, Thomson's plum pudding, Rutherford's nucleus and Bohr's energy levels, and what each experiment added.
5. Write ²³₁₁Na on the board. Show how to get protons (11), electrons (11) and neutrons (23 − 11 = 12). Introduce isotopes with ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.

## Class activity

In pairs, students complete a table of protons, neutrons and electrons for ¹²C, ¹⁴C, ¹⁶O, ²⁴Mg, ²⁷Al and ⁴⁰Ca.

## Evaluation

1. How many significant figures are in 0.0250 g?
2. What did Rutherford's experiment show about the atom?

## Assignment

Quiz questions 1 to 5, and read the section on Bohr's model.

reading.title: Measuring matter and looking inside the atom
reading.content:
# Measuring matter and looking inside the atom

Chemistry is an experimental science, so every chemist must measure well. In the laboratory you will measure **mass** with a balance (kilogram, kg, or gram, g), **length** with a metre rule (metre, m), **time** with a stopwatch (second, s), **temperature** with a thermometer (kelvin, K, or degree Celsius) and **volume** with a measuring cylinder, pipette or burette (cubic decimetre, dm³, or cubic centimetre, cm³).

## Significant figures, precision and accuracy

A reading should show every figure you are sure of plus one estimated figure. A burette reading of **24.50 cm³** has four significant figures. Zeros in front of a number do not count: **0.0250 g** has three.

- A set of readings is **precise** when the readings are close to one another.
- It is **accurate** when the readings are close to the true value.

A balance that has not been zeroed can give 4.62 g, 4.61 g and 4.62 g for a 5.00 g weight: precise, but not accurate.

## The scientific method

Scientists **observe**, suggest a **hypothesis** to explain what they see, test it by **experiment**, and when results agree again and again they state a **law**. A **theory** explains why the law holds.

## Models of the atom

- **Dalton (1808)** said matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms, and atoms of one element are identical. We now know atoms can be split and that isotopes of one element have different masses.
- **J.J. Thomson** discovered the electron with the cathode ray tube and pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons stuck in it.
- **Rutherford** fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected and very few bounced back. So the atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positive **nucleus**.
- **Bohr** placed the electrons in fixed **energy levels** (shells) around the nucleus.

## Symbols of atoms

An atom is written with its **mass number** (A) on top and its **atomic number** (Z) below: ²³₁₁Na.

- Atomic number = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom.
- Number of neutrons = A − Z.

**Worked example.** For ³⁵₁₇Cl: protons = 17, electrons = 17, neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18.

**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, such as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. They differ only in the number of neutrons.

2.topic: Relative atomic mass, particles of matter and electron configuration
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. define relative atomic mass and the atomic mass unit on the carbon-12 scale;
2. calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine from the abundance of its isotopes;
3. distinguish atoms, molecules and ions with examples;
4. classify changes as physical or chemical with reasons;
5. write the s, p, d electron configuration of the first thirty elements and describe the shapes of s and p orbitals.

## Materials

A periodic table chart, an iron nail and a bar magnet, common salt and water, a candle and matches, balloons to model s and p orbitals.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: if three bags of oranges weigh 2 kg, 2 kg and 5 kg, is the average 3 kg? What if there are 75 small bags and 25 big ones? Use this to lead to a weighted average.

## Development

1. Define the atomic mass unit as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Define relative atomic mass.
2. Work the chlorine example on the board: 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl gives 35.5. Students try boron (10.8).
3. Define atom, molecule and ion with examples (Na, O₂, Na⁺, Cl⁻).
4. Magnetise the nail, dissolve the salt, burn the candle. Students say which change is physical and which is chemical, and why.
5. Introduce shells as main energy levels and s, p, d as sub-levels holding 2, 6 and 10 electrons. Write configurations up to zinc, noting that 4s fills before 3d.
6. Use one balloon for the spherical s orbital and two tied balloons for the dumbbell p orbital.

## Class activity

Groups write the s, p, d configurations of Na, Cl, K, Ca, Fe and Zn and check each other's work.

## Evaluation

1. Why is the relative atomic mass of chlorine not a whole number?
2. Is rusting a physical or chemical change? Give one reason.

## Assignment

Problem set, due next lesson.

reading.content:
# Weighing atoms and arranging their electrons

## The carbon-12 scale

Atoms are far too light to weigh one at a time, so chemists compare them with a standard: the carbon-12 atom. One **atomic mass unit (amu)** is one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

The **relative atomic mass** of an element is the average mass of one of its atoms compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It has no unit.

## Why chlorine is 35.5

Natural chlorine is a mixture of two isotopes: 75% is ³⁵Cl and 25% is ³⁷Cl. The relative atomic mass is a weighted average:

Relative atomic mass = (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) / 100 = (2625 + 925) / 100 = **35.5**

No single chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5. It is the average of the mixture.

## Atoms, molecules and ions

- An **atom** is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction, e.g. Na, Fe.
- A **molecule** is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist on its own, made of atoms joined together, e.g. O₂, H₂O.
- An **ion** is a charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons, e.g. Na⁺, Cl⁻.

## Physical and chemical changes

In a **physical change** no new substance is formed and the change is easily reversed: melting shea butter, magnetising an iron nail, dissolving salt in water. In a **chemical change** a new substance forms and the change is not easily reversed: burning firewood, rusting of iron, leaves decaying on a farm.

## Electrons in sub-levels

Each main shell is divided into **sub-levels** called s, p and d. An s sub-level holds up to 2 electrons, a p up to 6 and a d up to 10. They fill in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d.

- ₁₁Na: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
- ₁₉K: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹ (4s is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first)
- ₂₆Fe: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²

An **s orbital** is spherical. A **p orbital** is dumbbell-shaped, and there are three of them, along the x, y and z axes.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. state the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle and use them to fill orbitals;
2. write full and abbreviated electron configurations;
3. find the group and period of an element from its configuration;
4. classify mixtures and choose a method to separate them;
5. use melting and boiling points as tests of purity.

## Materials

A mixture of sand, common salt and iodine; filter funnel and paper, evaporating dish, Bunsen burner or spirit lamp, separating funnel with kerosene and water, chalk and ink for chromatography, a magnet and iron filings, a chart of separation methods.

Show the class a cup of garri mixed with sand. Ask: how would your mother get the sand out? Collect answers and name the methods they describe.

reading.title: Rules for filling orbitals, and separating mixtures
reading.content:
# Rules for filling orbitals

Three rules decide where the electrons of an atom go.

- **Aufbau principle.** Electrons enter the orbitals of lowest energy first: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d.
- **Pauli exclusion principle.** An orbital holds at most two electrons, and the two must spin in opposite directions.
- **Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.** When there are several orbitals of the same energy, such as the three 2p orbitals, electrons go in singly before any pairing begins.

**Worked example.** Nitrogen has 7 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p³. The three 2p electrons sit one in each 2p orbital, all unpaired. Oxygen has one more, so one 2p orbital now holds a pair: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴, with two unpaired electrons.

## Abbreviated configurations

The inner electrons can be written as the noble gas before the element: sodium is [Ne] 3s¹ and calcium is [Ar] 4s².

## Configuration and the periodic table

The number of the outermost shell gives the **period**. The number of electrons in the outer s and p sub-levels gives the **group**. Chlorine, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵, has its outer electrons in shell 3 and seven of them, so it is in Period 3, Group 7.

# Mixtures and their separation

A **mixture** contains two or more substances not chemically combined. Mixtures can be solid-solid (sand and salt), solid-liquid (chalk in water), liquid-liquid (kerosene and water) or gas-gas (air).

| Method | Use it to separate |
| --- | --- |
| Sublimation | a solid that sublimes, such as iodine or ammonium chloride, from one that does not |
| Filtration | an insoluble solid from a liquid |
| Evaporation and crystallisation | a dissolved solid from its solution |
| Distillation | a liquid from a solution, e.g. pure water from salt water |
| Fractional distillation | miscible liquids with different boiling points |
| Separating funnel | immiscible liquids such as kerosene and water |
| Chromatography | the dyes in an ink |
| Magnet | iron filings from sand |
| Precipitation | an ion removed as an insoluble solid |

## Is it pure?

A pure solid melts sharply at a fixed temperature; benzoic acid melts at 122 °C. An impurity lowers the melting point and makes it melt over a range. A pure liquid boils at a fixed temperature; an impurity such as dissolved salt raises the boiling point.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. place metals, semi-metals and non-metals, the alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens and transition metals on the periodic table;
2. state the periodic law;
3. describe and explain the trends in atomic size, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity, including the beryllium-boron and nitrogen-oxygen exceptions;
4. describe the change from metallic to non-metallic character and from ionic to covalent compounds across a period;
5. write equations for the reactions of acids with Na, Mg, Al, K, Ca, their oxides and trioxocarbonates (IV), and state the pH of solutions of the metal oxides.

## Materials

A large periodic table chart, magnesium ribbon, marble chips, magnesium oxide, dilute hydrochloric acid, lime water, universal indicator and colour chart, test tubes, splints.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show a calendar. Ask: what repeats every seven days? Explain that the properties of elements repeat in the same way as atomic number increases.

2. Plot atomic radius and first ionisation energy across Period 2 on the board. Explain both trends with nuclear charge and shielding.
3. Explain the dips at boron (2p electron easier to remove than 2s) and oxygen (paired 2p electron repelled by its partner).

The practical: reactions of magnesium, magnesium oxide and marble chips with dilute hydrochloric acid.

2. Write the equation for magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid.

Complete the practical write-up with equations.

reading.content:
# Patterns in the periodic table

## The periodic law

The **periodic law** states that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. When elements are arranged in order of atomic number, similar properties come back at regular intervals.

Metals are on the left and in the middle; non-metals are on the right. Between them sit the **semi-metals** (metalloids) such as boron and silicon. Group 1 holds the **alkali metals**, Group 2 the **alkaline earth metals**, Group 7 the **halogens**, and the block between Groups 2 and 3 holds the **transition metals**.

## Trends across a period

From left to right the nuclear charge rises, but the new electrons go into the same shell. The outer electrons are pulled in more strongly, so:

- **atomic radius decreases**;
- **ionisation energy**, the energy to remove an electron from a gaseous atom, generally **increases**;
- **electron affinity** and **electronegativity** increase.

Down a group, atoms gain shells, so atomic radius increases and ionisation energy decreases.

### Two exceptions in Period 2

- **Boron is lower than beryllium.** Boron's outer electron is in 2p, which is higher in energy than beryllium's 2s, so it is easier to remove.
- **Oxygen is lower than nitrogen.** Nitrogen's three 2p electrons are unpaired. In oxygen one 2p orbital holds a pair, and repulsion within the pair makes one of them easier to remove.

## From metal to non-metal

Across Period 3, sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals, silicon is a semi-metal, and phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine are non-metals. Their chlorides change from ionic (NaCl) to covalent (PCl₃).

## Metals, oxides and trioxocarbonates with acids

Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen:

Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

Metal oxide + acid → salt + water:

CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O

Trioxocarbonate (IV) + acid → salt + water + carbon (IV) oxide:

Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

Potassium and sodium react with acid violently and are never used this way in the school laboratory. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop; carbon (IV) oxide turns lime water milky.

The oxides of Na, K and Ca dissolve to form strongly alkaline solutions (pH about 13). Magnesium oxide dissolves only slightly, giving a pH of about 9 to 10.

5.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe the trends in physical state, melting and boiling points and reactivity of the halogens;
2. explain displacement of one halogen by another as a redox reaction, and write the equations;
3. give the electron configurations of the first transition series and describe their characteristic properties;
4. compare the reactivity of transition metals with that of Li, Na, Be and Mg;
5. explain what a chemical bond is and draw Lewis dot structures for simple ionic and covalent compounds.

## Materials

Chlorine water, bromine water, aqueous potassium bromide and potassium iodide, test tubes, samples of copper (II) tetraoxosulphate (VI), iron (II) and iron (III) salts, an iron nail and a magnet, a chart of the halogens.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Show the class a bottle of household bleach and some iodine tincture from the first-aid box. Ask: what do these two have in common? Lead to the halogens.

## Development

1. Tabulate F₂ (pale yellow gas), Cl₂ (greenish-yellow gas), Br₂ (red-brown liquid) and I₂ (grey-black solid). Explain the rising melting points by stronger van der Waals forces between bigger molecules.
2. Add chlorine water to KBr and KI. Students record the colour changes. Explain that chlorine, the stronger oxidising agent, takes electrons from bromide and iodide ions. Show chlorine with water and with cold sodium hydroxide.
3. Write the configurations of Sc to Zn. Show the coloured salts, FeCl₂ and FeCl₃ as variable oxidation states, and iron as a catalyst and a magnetic metal.
4. Compare: sodium reacts violently with cold water, iron only rusts slowly or reacts with steam.
5. Define a chemical bond. Draw the Lewis structures of NaCl, MgO, H₂, H₂O and NH₃.

## Class activity

Pairs draw Lewis dot structures for KCl, CaO, HCl and CH₄ and say which are ionic and which are covalent.

## Evaluation

1. Why does chlorine displace iodine from potassium iodide?
2. Give two properties of transition metals with an example of each.

Worksheet, due Thursday.

reading.title: The halogens, the transition metals and chemical bonds
reading.content:
# The halogens

The halogens are the Group 7 elements: fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine. Each has seven outer electrons and needs one more to become stable, so all are reactive non-metals and oxidising agents.

| Halogen | State at room temperature | Colour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fluorine, F₂ | gas | pale yellow |
| Chlorine, Cl₂ | gas | greenish-yellow |
| Bromine, Br₂ | liquid | red-brown |
| Iodine, I₂ | solid | grey-black |

Down the group the molecules get bigger, the forces between them get stronger, and so melting and boiling points **increase**. Reactivity **decreases**: fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent, iodine the weakest. Halogens show oxidation states from −1 (in NaCl) to +1 (in NaOCl, bleach) and higher.

**Displacement.** A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt:

Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (the solution turns orange)

Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (the solution turns brown)

Chlorine gains electrons and is reduced; the bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised. Chlorine reacts with water to give HCl and HOCl, and with cold dilute sodium hydroxide to give the bleach NaOCl.

# The first transition series

The elements from scandium (21) to zinc (30) fill the 3d sub-level, e.g. Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². They are hard, dense, shiny metals with high melting points. Their characteristic properties are:

- **variable oxidation states**, e.g. FeCl₂ (+2) and FeCl₃ (+3);
- **coloured compounds**, e.g. blue CuSO₄·5H₂O, green iron (II) salts;
- **complex ions**, e.g. deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺;
- **catalytic activity**, e.g. iron in the Haber process, nickel in hardening palm oil into margarine;
- **paramagnetism**, from unpaired d electrons.

They are far less reactive than the s-block metals. Sodium fizzes about on cold water; iron does not react with cold water, rusts slowly in moist air and reacts only with steam when red hot.

# What is a chemical bond?

A **chemical bond** is the force that holds atoms together in a compound. Atoms bond to reach a stable outer shell, usually eight electrons. In a **Lewis dot structure** the outer electrons are shown as dots and crosses. In NaCl, sodium gives its one outer electron to chlorine, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (an ionic bond). In H₂O, oxygen shares one pair of electrons with each hydrogen atom (covalent bonds).

reading.title: How atoms hold together
reading.content:
# How atoms hold together

## Ionic bonds

An **ionic (electrovalent) bond** forms when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. Sodium (2,8,1) gives its outer electron to chlorine (2,8,7). Both reach a stable octet: Na⁺ is 2,8 and Cl⁻ is 2,8,8. The oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly.

Ionic bonding is favoured when:

- the metal has a **low ionisation energy** (it loses electrons easily);
- the non-metal has a **high electron affinity** (it releases energy when it gains electrons);
- the **electronegativity difference** between them is large.

### Properties of ionic compounds

The ions form a giant **lattice** held by strong forces, so ionic compounds:

- are hard, brittle crystalline solids with **high melting points** (NaCl melts at 801 °C);
- usually **dissolve in water** (a polar solvent) but not in kerosene (non-polar);
- **conduct electricity when molten or dissolved**, because the ions are then free to move, but not when solid.

### IUPAC names

The metal is named first. Where it has more than one oxidation state, the state is given in Roman numerals: FeCl₃ is iron (III) chloride. For oxoanions the number of oxygen atoms and the oxidation state of the central atom are both shown: KNO₃ is potassium trioxonitrate (V) and CuSO₄ is copper (II) tetraoxosulphate (VI).

## Covalent bonds

A **covalent bond** is a shared pair of electrons, one from each atom. It forms between non-metal atoms with similar, high electronegativities, which all need electrons. In water, oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen atom.

### Properties of simple covalent compounds

The bonds inside each molecule are strong, but the forces between molecules are weak, so:

- they have **low melting and boiling points** (candle wax, naphthalene);
- most dissolve in **non-polar solvents** like kerosene, not in water;
- they **do not conduct electricity**, because there are no ions.

## Coordinate (dative) covalent bonds

In a **dative bond** both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom. Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen. A hydrogen ion has no electrons at all. The nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺:

NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺

Once formed, the dative bond is just like the other three N–H bonds.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. predict the shapes of BeCl₂, BF₃, CH₄, NH₃ and CO₂ using electron-pair repulsion;
2. describe metallic bonding and explain how atomic radius, ionisation energy and the number of valence electrons affect its strength;
3. explain the typical properties of metals from metallic bonding;
4. distinguish polar from non-polar molecules and describe van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds;
5. explain the boiling point trends of the noble gases, halogens and alkanes, and the high boiling point of water compared with hydrogen sulphide.

## Materials

Balloons tied in twos, threes and fours, ball-and-stick models, a copper wire, an aluminium sheet, a hammer, a dry cell and bulb circuit, a burette of water and a charged plastic comb.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Tie two, three and four balloons together and let the class see how they spread out. Ask: why do they not stay bunched on one side?

## Development

1. Explain that electron pairs repel and spread out as far as possible. Build BeCl₂ (linear, 180°), BF₃ (trigonal planar, 120°), CH₄ (tetrahedral, 109.5°) and NH₃ (pyramidal, 107°). Note that CO₂ is linear.
2. Draw a lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons. Compare sodium and magnesium.
3. Use the model to explain conduction, malleability, ductility, lustre and sonority. Hammer the aluminium sheet and test the copper wire in the circuit.
4. Hold the charged comb near a thin stream of water to show water is polar.
5. Explain dipole-dipole, induced dipole and London forces. Tabulate the boiling points of He to Xe, F₂ to I₂ and methane to pentane.
6. Compare H₂O (100 °C) with H₂S (−60 °C) and explain hydrogen bonding.

## Class activity

Groups build the five molecules with models and record the shape and bond angle of each.

1. Why is magnesium harder than sodium?
2. Why is the bond angle in NH₃ less than 109.5°?

reading.title: Shapes, metals and the forces between molecules
reading.content:
# Shapes of molecules

The electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and move as far apart as possible. This decides the shape of the molecule.

| Molecule | Pairs on central atom | Shape | Bond angle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BeCl₂ | 2 bond pairs | linear | 180° |
| CO₂ | 2 double bonds | linear | 180° |
| BF₃ | 3 bond pairs | trigonal planar | 120° |
| CH₄ | 4 bond pairs | tetrahedral | 109.5° |
| NH₃ | 3 bond pairs, 1 lone pair | pyramidal | about 107° |

A lone pair repels more strongly than a bond pair, so it squeezes the N–H bonds in ammonia closer together than in methane.

# Metallic bonding

In a metal, the atoms give up their outer electrons. The result is a lattice of positive ions in a **sea of delocalised electrons**, which holds the ions together.

The bond is stronger when the atoms are small, when the ionisation energy is low enough for the electrons to be released, and when each atom gives more valence electrons. Magnesium gives two electrons per atom and sodium only one, so magnesium is harder and melts at 650 °C, against 98 °C for sodium.

The model explains the properties of metals:

- **conduction** of heat and electricity: the delocalised electrons move freely;
- **malleability and ductility**: layers of ions slide over one another while the electron sea holds them together;
- **lustre** and **sonority**: they shine when polished and ring when struck.

# Forces between molecules

In a **polar** molecule such as HCl, one end is slightly negative and the other slightly positive. **Van der Waals forces** are the weak attractions between molecules:

- **dipole-dipole** forces between polar molecules;
- **induced dipole-dipole** forces, when a polar molecule distorts a non-polar one;
- **induced dipole-induced dipole** (London) forces, present in all molecules, stronger in bigger molecules with more electrons.

That is why boiling points rise down the noble gases (He to Xe), down the halogens (F₂ to I₂) and along the alkanes (methane to pentane).

**Hydrogen bonds** are much stronger. They form when hydrogen is bonded to a very electronegative atom (N, O or F). Water boils at 100 °C, but hydrogen sulphide, a heavier molecule, boils at −60 °C, because sulphur is not electronegative enough for hydrogen bonding.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. compare ionic, covalent, dative, metallic and intermolecular bonds;
2. write the symbols of the first thirty elements and other common ones, and calculate the percentage composition of a compound;

reading.title: Counting atoms: formulae, equations and the mole
reading.content:
# Bonds compared

| Bond | Formed by | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ionic | transfer of electrons | NaCl |
| Covalent | sharing a pair, one electron from each atom | CH₄ |
| Dative | sharing a pair donated by one atom | NH₄⁺ |
| Metallic | ions in a sea of delocalised electrons | copper |
| Intermolecular | weak forces or hydrogen bonds between molecules | ice |

# Percentage composition

**Worked example.** Find the percentage of nitrogen in ammonium trioxonitrate (V), NH₄NO₃ (H = 1, N = 14, O = 16), a fertiliser sold in Kano.

Molar mass = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80 g mol⁻¹. Mass of nitrogen = 2 × 14 = 28 g.

Percentage of nitrogen = 28/80 × 100 = **35%**.

# Kinds of chemical equation

- **Combustion:** CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
- **Synthesis:** Fe + S → FeS
- **Displacement:** Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
- **Decomposition:** CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
- **Ionic:** Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)

# The laws of chemical combination

1. **Conservation of mass.** Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants, which is why every equation must balance.
2. **Constant composition.** All pure samples of a compound contain the same elements combined in the same proportion by mass. Copper (II) oxide is always 80% copper, however it is made.
3. **Multiple proportions.** When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. With 12 g of carbon, 16 g of oxygen gives CO and 32 g gives CO₂: a ratio of 1 : 2.

# The mole

A **mole** is the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles. This number is **Avogadro's constant**, L. The particles may be atoms, molecules, ions, formula units or electrons, so always say which.

The **molar mass** is the mass of one mole, in g mol⁻¹. Then:

amount (mol) = mass (g) / molar mass (g mol⁻¹)

number of particles = amount × L

**Worked example.** How many molecules are in 4.4 g of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16)? Molar mass = 44 g mol⁻¹, so amount = 4.4/44 = 0.1 mol. Molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = **6.02 × 10²²**.

10.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. use mole ratios from a balanced equation to find amounts, masses, volumes of solution and percentage yield;
2. describe a solution in terms of solute and solvent, and tell dilute from concentrated, and acidic, basic and neutral solutions;
3. express concentration in g dm⁻³ and mol dm⁻³ and convert between them;
4. explain the terms primary standard, secondary standard and standard solution, and prepare a standard solution of anhydrous Na₂CO₃;
5. prepare a dilute solution by dilution and work out the dilution factor;
6. state the postulates of the kinetic theory and use them to explain melting, boiling, evaporation, dissolution, Brownian motion and diffusion.

The practical: preparing a standard solution of sodium trioxocarbonate (IV) and diluting it.

reading.title: How much is dissolved? Concentration and standard solutions
reading.content:
# Solutions and concentration

A **solution** is a uniform mixture of a **solute** dissolved in a **solvent**. Salt water has salt as the solute and water as the solvent. A **dilute** solution has a little solute in a lot of solvent; a **concentrated** one has a lot. Solutions may be **acidic** (lime juice turns blue litmus red), **basic** (soap solution turns red litmus blue) or **neutral** (salt water does neither).

**Concentration** says how much solute is in each cubic decimetre (dm³, the same as a litre, 1000 cm³) of solution:

- **mass concentration** in g dm⁻³ = mass of solute / volume in dm³;
- **molar concentration** in mol dm⁻³ = amount of solute / volume in dm³;
- molar concentration = mass concentration / molar mass.

**Worked example.** 5.85 g of NaCl (molar mass 58.5 g mol⁻¹) is made up to 500 cm³. Mass concentration = 5.85/0.500 = 11.7 g dm⁻³. Molar concentration = 11.7/58.5 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³.

# Standard solutions

A **standard solution** is one whose concentration is known exactly. It is made from a **primary standard**: a substance that is pure, stable in air, not hygroscopic and has a known formula, so it can be weighed accurately. Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ and oxalic acid, (COOH)₂·2H₂O, are primary standards. Sodium hydroxide is not: it absorbs water and carbon (IV) oxide from the air. Its solution is a **secondary standard**, found by titrating it against a primary standard.

# Dilution

Adding water does not change the amount of solute, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Making 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ Na₂CO₃ up to 250 cm³ gives 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. The **dilution factor** is 250/25.0 = 10.

# Mole ratios and yield

**Worked example.** Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. How much ZnCl₂ can 6.5 g of zinc give (Zn = 65, Cl = 35.5)? Amount of Zn = 6.5/65 = 0.10 mol. The ratio Zn : ZnCl₂ is 1 : 1, so 0.10 mol ZnCl₂ = 0.10 × 136 = 13.6 g. If only 11.56 g is collected, the **percentage yield** is 11.56/13.6 × 100 = 85%.

# The kinetic theory

All matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion. Their average kinetic energy rises with temperature. Particles of a gas are far apart and their collisions are perfectly elastic. Melting happens when particles vibrate enough to leave their fixed positions; evaporation when fast particles escape from the surface; boiling when particles escape from all through the liquid. Diffusion and Brownian motion are evidence of this motion.

writeUps.text: We weighed 2.65 g of sodium carbonate and dissolved it in water in the volumetric flask, then filled it to the line. Mass concentration = 2.65/250 = 0.0106 g/cm3. Molar mass = 106. Molar concentration = 2.65/106 = 0.025 mol/dm3. We diluted 25 cm3 to 250 cm3 so it is 10 times weaker.
writeUps.feedback: Your molar mass and dilution idea are right. Dissolve the solid in a beaker first and rinse it into the flask. 0.025 is the number of moles, which are in 0.250 dm³, so the concentration is 0.100 mol dm⁻³; and give the diluted value, 0.0100 mol dm⁻³.

writeUps.text: 2.70 g of $\ce{Na2CO3}$ was dissolved in a beaker of distilled water and poured into the 250 cm3 flask, and the beaker was rinsed into it. Water was added up to the mark. Mass concentration = 2.70/0.25 = 10.8 g/dm3. Molar concentration = 10.8/106 = 0.102 mol/dm3. After dilution it is 0.102 mol/dm3 because the amount of salt does not change.
writeUps.feedback: Good technique and correct concentrations for your mass. The amount of salt stays the same, but it is now in ten times the volume, so the concentration falls ten times, to 0.0102 mol dm⁻³. Say the dilution factor is 10.
